name: Atopic eczema
definition: A skin condition that causes dry, itchy skin and comes and goes in flare-ups.
overview: Atopic eczema is a skin condition whose main sign is itchy, dry skin. The National Eczema Society says it affects 1 in 5 children and 1 in 10 adults in the UK. It usually begins in early childhood, often in the first year of life. It tends to flare up and settle, and the NHS says there is currently no cure, although symptoms tend to get better with age.
causes: The exact cause is not always known.
Genetics, a weakened skin barrier, environmental exposures and immune system problems are thought to contribute.
riskFactors: A family history of the condition raises the risk.
Changes in the filaggrin gene are among the factors most often linked to it.
Exposure to pets, house-dust mites and pollen is thought to play a role.
signs: The skin can be dry, cracked, scaly, thickened, blistered or bleeding.
The affected skin may look red, white, purple or grey, or lighter or darker than the skin around it.
Scratching can make the skin bleed and lead to secondary infection.
complications: Itching and scratching can disturb sleep.
Skin infections can develop, including bacterial infection with Staphylococcus aureus and fungal infections.
Herpes simplex virus can spread widely over eczema skin, a serious problem called eczema herpeticum.
Children with atopic eczema often develop asthma or allergic rhinitis, and food allergy is sometimes linked, particularly in very young children.
Missing school, depression and reduced self-confidence are listed effects.
diagnosis: There is no conclusive laboratory test for atopic eczema, so it is a clinical diagnosis. A clinician assesses the pattern, onset and severity of the eczema and its effect on the person and family. Most children with mild atopic eczema do not need allergy tests.
treatment: There is currently no cure, but treatments can help manage the condition and improve symptoms. Emollients (moisturisers) are the first-line treatment during both flares and remissions, with topical corticosteroid creams as the other main option. A pharmacist can advise in mild cases, and a GP can prescribe treatments or refer the person to a skin specialist (dermatologist) when it is more severe. Specialist options include phototherapy and immune-suppressing medicines.
prevention: Flares can be reduced by keeping skin moisturised, avoiding known triggers such as soaps and detergents, and keeping cool.
seekCare: A routine GP appointment is the route when symptoms appear or treatments are not helping. An urgent GP appointment or a call to NHS 111 is advised if the skin is blistered, crusty, leaking fluid or pus, painful, swollen or warm, suddenly worse, or there is a high temperature or the person feels generally unwell. For suspected eczema herpeticum, the National Eczema Society advises seeing a doctor immediately, and using NHS 111 or the nearest A&E if the GP cannot see the person. Call 999 for anyone who is seriously unwell, struggling to breathe or hard to wake.

sections.heading: What does atopic eczema look and feel like?
sections.body:
Itchy, dry skin is the main sign of atopic eczema. The skin can also crack, scale, thicken, blister or bleed. Affected areas may look red, white, purple or grey, or lighter or darker than the surrounding skin.

The condition comes and goes, with flare-ups when the skin gets worse. NICE describes it as an episodic disease of flares and remissions, and in severe cases the activity may be continuous. Itching can lead to a cycle of regular scratching, which can affect sleep, make the skin bleed and allow infection to set in. The National Eczema Society notes that the itch can become almost unbearable, especially at night. It also says many children and adults have related sleeplessness, anxiety, depression and other mental health problems.

sections.heading: What causes it, and what sets off flares?
sections.body:
The exact cause is not always clear. Genetics, a weakened skin barrier, exposures such as pets, house-dust mites and pollen, and immune system problems are all thought to play a part. A family history raises the risk, and changes in the filaggrin gene are among the factors most often linked to the condition.

The NHS lists common triggers as soaps, washing detergents, some fabrics, pets, pollen, house-dust mites, heat, stress and skin infections. The British Association of Dermatologists also names dust and woollen clothing as possible triggers. Infections are also a factor, and the cold sore virus can cause a sudden, painful, widespread flare-up with weeping small sores. NICE says the role of stress, humidity and temperature extremes in causing flares is unclear, but they are best avoided where possible.

sections.heading: How is atopic eczema diagnosed?
sections.body:
There is no conclusive laboratory test for atopic eczema, so doctors diagnose it from the skin and the history. A clinician looks at the pattern, the age of onset and the severity of the eczema, and at its effect on the person and family. Most children with mild atopic eczema do not need allergy tests. Testing is considered in specific cases, such as seasonal flares, or asthma or hay fever alongside the eczema.

Referral to a specialist may follow when the diagnosis is uncertain, the eczema is not controlled with current treatment, or there is a high risk of complications. The NHS says a GP may also refer to an immunologist or paediatrician if corticosteroid tablets might be needed repeatedly or for a long time.

sections.heading: How is it treated?
sections.body:
There is currently no cure, but treatments can help manage atopic eczema and improve symptoms. Emollients, which are moisturisers, are the first-line treatment during both flares and remissions. The NHS advises continuing moisturiser even when the skin improves, and washing with an emollient instead of soap. Topical corticosteroid creams are the other main treatment the NHS names. The British Association of Dermatologists says topical calcineurin inhibitors can help prevent flare-ups when used regularly. Emollients can make fabrics flammable, so smoking and naked flames are best avoided near them.

Cotton bandages or clothing worn over creams can stop them rubbing off and help prevent direct scratching. Phototherapy uses ultraviolet light and is a second-line option for moderate to severe eczema, available only at specialist clinics or hospitals. Other specialist options include immune-suppressing tablets or syrups such as methotrexate and ciclosporin, and newer medicines given by injection or as tablets.

sections.heading: Living with atopic eczema and the outlook
sections.body:
The NHS says keeping cool helps, because heat worsens itching. The British Association of Dermatologists suggests comfortable clothes made of materials such as cotton and silk, and avoiding wool next to the skin. Its leaflet adds that scratching may feel good briefly but makes the skin itchier and worse in the long term. The NHS says diet should not be changed unless a doctor advises it.

The NHS says symptoms tend to get better as people get older. NICE says many children improve over time, but not all grow out of it, and it may get worse in teenage or adult life. NICE also notes that the tendency to dry, irritable skin generally persists and later recurrences are common.

sections.heading: When should someone get medical help?
sections.body:
A GP appointment is the route when symptoms appear or treatments are not helping. An urgent GP appointment or a call to NHS 111 is advised if the skin is blistered, crusty, leaking fluid or pus, painful, swollen or warm, or suddenly worse. The same applies to a high temperature or feeling generally unwell. These can signal infection or eczema herpeticum, which needs prompt treatment.

NICE describes eczema herpeticum as rapidly worsening, painful eczema with clustered blisters and punched-out sores. The National Eczema Society advises seeing a doctor immediately if it is suspected, with NHS 111 or the nearest A&E if the GP cannot see the person. NICE CKS says clinicians should arrange immediate hospital admission if it is suspected. Anyone who is seriously unwell, struggling to breathe or hard to wake needs a 999 call.

faqs.a: There is currently no cure for atopic eczema, according to the NHS. Treatments can help manage it and improve symptoms, and symptoms tend to get better with age. NICE notes that many children improve over time, but not all grow out of it, and it may get worse in teenage or adult life.

The National Eczema Society says it affects 1 in 5 children and 1 in 10 adults in the UK. NICE gives wider ranges, suggesting as many as 15% to 20% of school-age children and 2% to 10% of adults. In most people it begins in early childhood, often in the first year of life.

faqs.q: What is the first treatment for atopic eczema?
faqs.a: Emollients (moisturisers) are the first-line treatment, during both flares and remissions, according to NICE CKS. The NHS advises continuing moisturiser even when the skin improves, and washing with an emollient instead of soap. Topical corticosteroid creams are the other main option, and a pharmacist can advise in mild cases.

faqs.q: Does atopic eczema affect sleep and mood?
faqs.a: It can, because the NHS notes that scratching can affect sleep. The National Eczema Society says many children and adults have related sleeplessness, anxiety, depression and other mental health problems. NICE adds that sleep disturbance is common, especially during flare-ups, and can lead to irritability and poor concentration.

faqs.q: Is atopic eczema linked to asthma and hay fever?
faqs.a: NICE says children with atopic eczema often develop asthma or allergic rhinitis, and food allergy is sometimes linked, particularly in very young children. Most children with mild atopic eczema do not need allergy tests, which are considered only in specific cases.
